title: Strat Chat: Revision Programs
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien argues that the common default of telling students to revise independently widens the gap between strong and weak students. He describes how the strongest students demand feedback, the middle band busily re-reads and highlights, and the lowest band treats the time as free time. In place of vague instructions such as make a mind map or do what works for you, he lays out a structured revision program built on four ideas. The first is using question-level assessment data to re-teach the weakest areas and then revisit them at spaced intervals, since 95 percent success on one lesson fell to 70 percent in the next class. The second is mining the state assessors' reports for common misconceptions. The third is varying the lesson into short blocks of retrieval, timed application and low-stakes contests, and the fourth is making students rewrite responses so feedback is actually used.
points: Unstructured independent revision tends to benefit the strongest students and leave the lowest band idle, so teachers should own the structure of revision.
Teachers should use question-by-question assessment data to choose what to re-teach, because students practise what they are already good at.
A drop from 95 percent to 70 percent understanding between two classes shows why revised content must keep returning through spaced do-nows until the exam.
Assessors' reports reveal recurring misconceptions that are often tested again, so one or two lessons on them pay off.
Rewriting responses after feedback, including improving an imperfect model answer, turns feedback into durable learning.
quotes: Your middle band of students do what they think is effective revision, they click through slide decks, re-read and highlight their notes. They certainly are busy but they are not making significant progress.

One of the biggest mistakes we make as humans is that we too often practice the things we are good at. It makes sense. It feels great to be good at something and practicing what we are less confident in is scary as we may get something wrong.

We cannot possibly rely on teenagers to reflect on their areas of weakness and re-teach themselves the content and magically improve. It is our responsibility as teachers to use the data sources available to us (often summative assessment data) to make informed decisions about the areas of most need for students.

I followed this exact method with a class last year and on the independent question 95% of students showed clear understanding. Then I launched the next class with a do now about the exact same content and the number had fallen to 70%.

Using this information to inform a revision lesson or two exploring the specific misconceptions as well as how to respond to exam style questions about them can provide significant bang for your buck in terms of student achievement.

In my current school our double periods go for 2 hours and maintaining student attention for 2 hours on pure revision is a fruitless task. This means that I will often attempt to structure the session into either 2, 60 minute or 3, 40 minute blocks to keep the students focussed throughout the lesson.
Reading feedback alone does very little for student improvement unless they action it.
